q: On 28 June 2021, the Supreme Court held that persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotion under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, 1950, in the case of:
options: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph
State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas
solution:
The correct answer is State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph. Key Points

• The Supreme Court of India in its judgment on 28 June 2021 in the case of "State of Kerala vs Leesamma Joseph" affirmed that persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotion under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, 1950.

• While examining the constitutionality of Section 33 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, the Court noted that 'equality of opportunity' in matters of public employment includes provision of certain reservations in favour of persons with disabilities.

• Furthermore, it held that Article 16(4) of the Constitution, empowering the State to make provisions for reservation in matters of promotion in favour of any backward class of citizens, also includes persons with disabilities within its scope, regardless of the nature of their establishments, whether they belong to the public sector or the private sector.

The case of "Indra Sawhney v. Union of India" is popularly known as the "Mandal Commission case." It is a landmark judgment by the Supreme Court of India that dealt with the implementation of reservations for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in public employment. The Mandal Commission, officially known as the Second Backward Classes Commission, had recommended a reservation of 27% for OBCs in government jobs. The case involved a constitutional challenge to the implementation of these reservations.

Additional Information

• Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPDA):

• This is the principal legislation that protects the rights of individuals with disabilities in India.

• It replaces and strengthens the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995.

• The RPDA complies with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to which India is a signatory.

• The Act expands the list of recognized disabilities from 7 to 21, and mandates the central and state governments to take measures to ensure that persons with disabilities fully enjoy all human rights and fundamental freedoms.

• Section 33 of the RPDA states that the appropriate Governments shall appoint in every Government establishment, not less than four percent of the total number of vacancies in the cadre strength in each group of posts meant to be filled with persons with benchmark disabilities of which, one percent each shall be reserved for persons with benchmark disabilities under clauses (a), (b) and (c) and one percent for persons with benchmark disabilities under clauses (d) and (e), namely:—

• a. blindness and low vision;

• b. deaf and hard of hearing;

• c. locomotor disability including cerebral palsy, leprosy cured, dwarfism, acid attack victims and muscular dystrophy;

• d. autism, intellectual disability, specific learning disability and mental illness;

• e. multiple disabilities from amongst persons under clauses (a) to (d) including deaf-blindness.

• Article 16 of the Constitution of India generally provides for equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. However, clause 16(4) empowers the State to make provisions for reservation in appointments or posts in favor of any backward class of citizens if it believes they are not adequately represented in the services under the State.

• In the case "State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph" passed on 28 June 2021, the Supreme Court of India held that persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotions under Article 16(4) of the Constitution. This was a significant judgment reinforcing the principle of equal opportunities for persons with disabilities in public employment.

• The MPI assesses poverty at the individual level by considering various factors like nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets.

• HDI scores are used to assess and compare the level of human development across countries and regions.

q: Which Bill was passed by the Parliament, in July 2021, to help in the availability of working capital for the micro, small and medium enterprises sector?
options: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2021
solution:
The correct answer is The Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Bill, 2021.

Key Points

• The Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Bill, 2021 was introduced to address the challenges faced by the micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in accessing working capital.

• Factoring is a financial transaction where a business sells its accounts receivable (invoices) to a third party (called a factor) at a discount in exchange for immediate money.

• This amendment widens the scope of entities that can undertake factoring business, thereby increasing the availability of funds to the MSME sector.

• The Bill aims to simplify the operational constraints in the factoring business and make it more accessible and affordable for MSMEs.

Additional Information

• The Essential Commodities (Amendment) Bill, 2020

• This bill aims to deregulate the production, supply, distribution, and trade of certain food items to increase the competitiveness of the market.

• It seeks to remove commodities like cereals, pulses, oilseeds, edible oils, onions, and potatoes from the list of essential commodities.

• This deregulation is expected to attract private sector/foreign direct investment into the agriculture sector.

• The Minerals Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2020

• This bill aims to promote ease of doing business in the coal and mining sector by amending the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015.

• It allows companies to participate in auctions of coal and lignite blocks even without prior experience in coal mining.

• The bill also removes the restriction on end-use of minerals produced from coal and lignite blocks.

• The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2021

• This bill introduces a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP) for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

• PIRP is a quicker and cost-effective alternative to the normal Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

• This process allows MSMEs to restructure their liabilities and continue their business operations without undergoing a full insolvency process.

q: Which payload monitors solar wind at L1?

• The payload helps in understanding the interaction of solar wind with Earth’s magnetosphere and its impact on space weather.

• ASPEX provides critical data on the dynamics of solar wind, enabling scientists to predict geomagnetic storms and their potential effects on satellites, power grids, and communication systems.

• It plays a crucial role in enhancing our understanding of heliophysics and solar-terrestrial interactions by analyzing the solar wind in real-time from a vantage point at L1.

• SUIT also measures solar irradiance variations in the UV band, which have implications for Earth’s climate and atmospheric processes.

• SoLEXS is a payload on Aditya-L1 that observes X-ray emissions from the Sun.

• It monitors solar flares and estimates their energy output, providing insights into the Sun’s high-energy processes.

• The data from SoLEXS help in understanding the heating mechanisms of the Sun’s corona and its impact on the heliosphere.

• HEL1OS (High Energy L1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer):

q: Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, what is required for digital evidence to be presented in court?

It must be verified by a government official before submission
solution:

Key Points

• Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Indian Evidence Act), digital evidence must be accompanied by a valid digital signature to ensure its authenticity and integrity.

• A digital signature acts as a cryptographic mechanism that verifies the sender's identity and ensures that the data has not been altered during transmission.

• The requirement of a digital signature is in alignment with the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which governs digital transactions and electronic records in India.

• Courts accept digital evidence only when it has been properly authenticated and complies with the procedural requirements outlined in the Act.

• This measure ensures that the digital evidence presented in court is reliable and free from tampering or forgery.

• Digital evidence does not need to be converted into hard copy form for submission in court as per modern evidence laws.

• Hard copies may be used for reference but are not mandatory for the admissibility of digital evidence.

• Option 2: It must come from a reliable, government-approved platform

• While platforms may be regulated or approved by the government for specific purposes, digital evidence does not have to originate from such platforms to be admissible.

• The authenticity of the evidence is determined by its compliance with legal requirements, including the presence of valid digital signatures and adherence to prescribed procedures.

• Option 4: It must be verified by a government official before submission

• Digital evidence does not necessarily need to be verified by a government official before submission in court.

• Instead, its admissibility depends on factors such as authenticity, relevance, and compliance with procedural requirements, including digital signatures.

• Verification may be required in specific cases, but it is not a blanket rule under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

• Key Concepts Related to Digital Evidence:

• Digital evidence includes any information stored or transmitted in digital form that may be used in a court of law.

• Examples include emails, social media content, CCTV footage, electronic contracts, and mobile phone data.

• Authentication procedures, such as digital signatures and hash values, are crucial for ensuring the reliability of digital evidence.

• The Information Technology Act, 2000, and related amendments play a significant role in governing the use and admissibility of electronic records in India.

q: Which law replaced the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860?
solution:
The correct answer is Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Key Points

• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is the proposed law introduced to replace the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, which was a colonial-era legislation enacted during British rule.

• This new legislation aims to modernize the criminal justice system in India by making it more aligned with contemporary societal needs, values, and constitutional principles.

• One of its key objectives is to eliminate colonial influences and ensure a more victim-centric and citizen-friendly approach to justice delivery.

• The bill incorporates provisions for speedy trials, stringent punishment for crimes against women and children, and promotes the use of technology in the judicial process.

Additional Information

• Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860:

• The Indian Penal Code was enacted in 1860 and came into force in 1862 during British rule in India.

• It served as the primary criminal code in India, defining various crimes and their corresponding punishments.

• The IPC was drafted by the first Law Commission of India under the chairmanship of Lord Macaulay.

• Key Features of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita:

• It abolishes outdated provisions that were irrelevant in the current legal context.

• It introduces stringent punishments for crimes such as mob lynching, sexual crimes, and crimes against children.

• The bill promotes the use of modern technology in investigations and trials, such as video recordings and electronic evidence.

• It also emphasizes the protection of the rights of victims and witnesses in the legal process.

• Other Related Bills:

• Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita: Replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, focusing on procedural reforms to ensure speedier justice.

• Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam: Replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, aiming to update laws related to evidence gathering and admissibility in court proceedings.

• Rationale Behind the New Laws:

• The purpose of these reforms is to remove the colonial legacy and align the laws with the democratic ethos of modern India.

• It seeks to reduce delays in the justice delivery system and ensure transparency and accountability.

Important Points

• Need for Reform: The IPC was enacted in colonial times and contains outdated laws that are no longer relevant in modern India. The new laws aim to address these gaps.

• Victim-Centric Approach: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita introduces provisions to make the justice system more focused on the rights and needs of victims of crimes.

• Use of Technology: The new law encourages the use of technology in judicial processes, such as electronic communication and digital evidence.

• Recent Example: The introduction of these new laws in 2023 marks a significant step toward legal modernization in India, replacing three key colonial-era laws.

q: What is one of the major reforms introduced in BNSS, 2023 with respect to FIRs?

FIRs can only be filed physically at police stations
solution:

• BNSS 2023 introduced the provision for filing E-FIRs (Electronic First Information Reports) for specific offenses, making it more convenient for citizens to report crimes without visiting a police station.

• E-FIRs are primarily applicable for non-cognizable offenses (such as property theft up to a certain value or lost documents), reducing the burden on physical police infrastructure.

• This reform is aimed at increasing the accessibility and efficiency of the justice system, enabling quicker responses and reducing procedural delays.

• The online portal for filing E-FIRs is integrated with state and central crime databases, ensuring better coordination between law enforcement agencies.

• Strict protocols have been established to verify the authenticity of E-FIRs and to prevent misuse, such as requiring identity proof and OTP-based verification during the filing process.

Additional Information

• First Information Report (FIR):

• An FIR is a document prepared by the police when they receive information about the commission of a cognizable offense.

• Under Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), the police are mandated to register an FIR for cognizable offenses such as murder, theft, or kidnapping.

• The FIR acts as a formal complaint and serves as the basis for initiating an investigation.

• E-FIR System:

• E-FIR is a digital initiative to allow the public to report minor offenses online, without visiting a police station.

• It is part of the government's broader push for e-governance and the use of technology to enhance public service delivery.

• E-FIR services are currently available in many states in India, like Delhi, Maharashtra, and Karnataka, through designated portals.

• Cognizable vs. Non-Cognizable Offenses:

• Cognizable offenses are more severe crimes (e.g., murder, rape) where police can register an FIR and start an investigation without prior approval from a magistrate.

• Non-cognizable offenses are minor crimes (e.g., public nuisance, verbal abuse) where police need permission from a magistrate to investigate.

• Advantages of E-FIR:

• Convenience for citizens, especially in urban and remote areas.

• Reduction in paperwork and faster processing of complaints.

• Enhances transparency and accountability in the registration of complaints.

• Challenges of E-FIR:

• Risk of misuse or filing false complaints due to the lack of in-person verification.

• Dependence on digital literacy and access to technology, which may exclude certain sections of the population.

• Need for robust cybersecurity measures to protect sensitive data and prevent breaches.

Important Points

• Procedure for Filing an E-FIR:

• Log in to the state police department's official portal or mobile application.

• Fill out the required details, such as personal information and a description of the incident.

• Upload supporting documents or evidence, such as scanned copies of lost items or crime scenes.

• Complete the identity verification process via OTP or Aadhaar-based authentication.

• Once submitted, the E-FIR is reviewed by the concerned police department, and further action is initiated.

• Relevant Legal Provisions:

• Section 154 of the CrPC governs the registration of FIRs in India.

• E-FIRs do not replace traditional FIRs; they are an additional mechanism to simplify the process for specific offenses.

q: When was the concept of QUAD first proposed?
solution:
The correct answer is 2007.

Key Points

• The concept of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD) was first proposed in 2007 by the then Prime Minister of Japan, Shinzo Abe.

• The QUAD is a strategic dialogue between India, the United States, Japan, and Australia, aimed at promoting a free, open, and inclusive Indo-Pacific region.

• The idea was initially discussed in the context of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, where these four nations coordinated disaster relief efforts, but it formally took shape in 2007.

• This initiative was driven by concerns over the rise of China's influence in the Indo-Pacific region and the need for collaborative efforts to ensure regional security and stability.

• Although the QUAD lost momentum after its initial proposal in 2007, it was revived in 2017 due to growing geopolitical tensions and shared concerns about regional challenges.

Additional Information

• Structure and Objectives of QUAD:

• The QUAD is not a formal military alliance but a strategic forum that focuses on dialogue and cooperation in areas such as maritime security, counter-terrorism, climate change, and infrastructure development.

• It aims to promote a rules-based international order in the Indo-Pacific region.

• Key Events in QUAD's History:

• The first formal meeting of the QUAD took place in 2007 on the sidelines of the ASEAN Regional Forum in Manila.

• The group was revived in 2017 during the East Asia Summit in the Philippines, reflecting renewed interest in countering regional challenges.

• China's Response to QUAD:

• China has often criticized the QUAD, viewing it as an attempt to contain its influence in the Indo-Pacific region.

• Chinese officials have referred to the grouping as an "Asian NATO," though QUAD members have clarified that the forum is not a military alliance.

• Recent Developments:

• In 2021, the QUAD held its first-ever summit, attended virtually by the leaders of the four member nations, focusing on vaccine distribution, climate change, and emerging technologies.

• The QUAD has also emphasized maritime security and freedom of navigation in the South China Sea.

Important Points

• 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami:

• The collaboration between India, the US, Japan, and Australia during the 2004 tsunami relief efforts laid the foundation for future discussions on multilateral cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region.

• Shinzo Abe's Vision:

• In 2007, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe articulated the concept of a "confluence of the two seas," emphasizing the need for cooperation between the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

• Key Challenges:

• Despite its strategic importance, the QUAD faces challenges such as differing national interests among its members and China's growing assertiveness.

q: The Corruption Perception Index (CPI) 2024 is released by which global civil society organization?
solution:
The correct answer is Transparency International.

Key Points

• Transparency International is a global civil society organization established in 1993 to combat corruption worldwide and promote transparency, accountability, and integrity at all levels of government and society.
• The Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI), released annually by Transparency International, measures the perceived levels of public sector corruption in different countries and territories worldwide.
• The CPI uses a scale from 0 to 100, where 0 indicates a highly corrupt country and 100 indicates a very clean country. It is widely regarded as a key indicator for understanding global corruption trends.
• The index is compiled using data from 13 independent surveys and expert assessments conducted by reputable institutions globally. These sources assess factors like bribery, misuse of public office, and the effectiveness of anti-corruption policies.
• The CPI 2024 provides insights into corruption perception rankings for nearly 180 countries and territories, highlighting areas requiring attention for anti-corruption reforms and good governance.
Additional Information

• Transparency International:
• Headquartered in Berlin, Germany, Transparency International operates globally to fight corruption and promote transparency.
• It works closely with governments, businesses, and civil society to implement reforms aimed at reducing corruption risks.
• The organization is known for its advocacy, research, and public campaigns to promote integrity and ethical governance.
• Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI):
• The CPI is based on a composite of expert opinions and surveys from organizations such as the World Bank, World Economic Forum, and Economist Intelligence Unit.
• Countries with higher scores generally have stronger institutions, better governance, and more robust anti-corruption frameworks.
• Examples of countries consistently scoring high on the CPI include Denmark, Finland, and New Zealand, while countries like Somalia, Syria, and South Sudan often rank lower.
• Other Organizations Related to Global Governance:
• World Bank: Focuses on economic development and poverty alleviation globally. It does not specifically release indices like the CPI.
• UNODC (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime): Primarily tackles issues like drug trafficking, transnational organized crime, and corruption through its programs.
• OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development): Promotes policies to improve economic and social well-being. It publishes reports on anti-corruption practices but does not release the CPI.
• Important Points About Corruption:
• Corruption undermines economic growth, democracy, and social justice, leading to inefficiencies and inequalities.
• Effective anti-corruption strategies include strengthening institutions, enforcing laws, and promoting transparency in public and private sectors.
• International conventions such as the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) provide a framework for countries to combat corruption collectively.
